name: Applying for Government Jobs (USAJOBS)
objectives: Given a federal job announcement and your own background, identify the hiring paths you may qualify for and check whether a job is open to you, by reading the "This job is open to" section correctly

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding a federal job that is open to you

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How federal hiring works and your hiring paths
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the hiring paths you may qualify for and check who a job is open to.
This lesson builds toward: Given a federal job announcement and your own background, you will identify the hiring paths you may qualify for and check whether a job is open to you, by reading the "This job is open to" section correctly.
Federal jobs are posted on USAJOBS, the official site run by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Each posting is called a job announcement. Each agency (for example the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Forest Service or the IRS) reads applications and decides who qualifies.
Every announcement says who may apply, in a part called "This job is open to". USAJOBS groups applicants into hiring paths. Some of them: Open to the public (U.S. citizens and nationals), Veterans, Military spouses, Individuals with disabilities, Students, Recent graduates, Federal employees, and National Guard and reserves.
If a job is open only to federal employees and you are not one, your application will not be considered, however good it is. So always check this part first. Some special paths have their own rules: for example people with disabilities may apply under Schedule A with a proof-of-disability letter, and veterans may have veterans' preference.
Pay for many office and professional jobs uses the General Schedule (GS): 15 grades, from GS-1 to GS-15, each with 10 steps, plus locality pay that depends on where you work. Many trade and labor jobs use a different scale, the Federal Wage System (often shown as WG).
Step by step:
- Write down which hiring paths might fit you: public, veteran, military spouse, disability, student, recent graduate or another.
- Open an announcement and find "This job is open to".
- Check that at least one path listed fits you.
- If none fits, skip that job and find another.
Words to know:
- USAJOBS: the official, free website where U.S. federal jobs are posted.
- OPM: the Office of Personnel Management, the agency that runs federal hiring rules and USAJOBS.
- Job announcement: the full job posting: who can apply, duties, qualifications, pay and how to apply.
- Hiring path: a group of people a job is open to, such as the public, veterans or students.
- Schedule A: a hiring authority that lets agencies hire people with disabilities without the usual competition.
- General Schedule (GS): the main federal pay scale, with grades GS-1 to GS-15 and 10 steps in each grade.
- Locality pay: extra pay that depends on the area where the job is.
Official sources:
- USAJOBS: Explore hiring paths
- USAJOBS: Open to the public
- OPM: General Schedule
Try it now: On paper, list every hiring path that might fit you and why (for example: "Open to the public: I am a U.S. citizen" or "Veterans: I served in the Army"). Then open usajobs.gov/hiringpath and read the page for each path on your list.
You can now name the hiring paths that may fit you and check whether a federal job is open to you before you spend time on it.

check.q: An announcement says "This job is open to: Federal employees - competitive service". You have never worked for the government. What do you do?
options: Apply anyway with a strong resume
Call the agency to ask for an exception
Skip it and find a job open to the public
Apply under a friend's federal status
check.why: If no listed path fits you, the application will not be considered, so your time is better spent on a job open to you.

check.q: Which hiring path is for U.S. citizens and nationals in general?
options: Special authorities
Senior executives
Federal employees
Open to the public
check.why: "Open to the public" is the path for U.S. citizens and nationals in general.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting up USAJOBS and searching smart
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a USAJOBS profile and save a filtered job search.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone or a library computer, you will create a USAJOBS profile and save a job search filtered by location, pay grade and hiring path, using only the official usajobs.gov site and paying no one.
Go to usajobs.gov and choose to create a profile. USAJOBS uses Login.gov, the government's sign-in service, so you set up a Login.gov account with your email, a strong password and a second sign-in step (such as a code sent to your phone). Type the address yourself; do not follow links in texts or ads.
In your profile you add your contact details and answer questions about yourself, such as whether you are a veteran or a current federal employee. These answers help USAJOBS show you the hiring paths that fit you. The profile is also where your resumes and documents are stored.
To search, type a job word or skill (for example "maintenance", "customer service" or "medical support") and a city or state. Then use the filters: location, pay grade, hiring path, work schedule (full-time or part-time), and remote or telework if you want them. When the results look right, save the search so USAJOBS can email you new jobs.
Using USAJOBS is free. No real government office charges you to create a profile, search or apply.
Step by step:
- Type usajobs.gov into the browser yourself.
- Create a profile and sign in through Login.gov.
- Fill in your profile, including the questions about veterans' status and federal service.
- Search with a job word and a location.
- Add filters: pay grade, hiring path, schedule.
- Save the search and turn on email alerts.
Words to know:
- Profile: your USAJOBS account page, where your details, resumes and documents are kept.
- Login.gov: the U.S. government's sign-in service, used to sign in to USAJOBS and other government sites.
- Filter: a setting that narrows search results, such as location or pay grade.
- Saved search: a search USAJOBS remembers and uses to email you new jobs that match.
- Telework: working from home some or all of the time.
Official sources:
- USAJOBS
- Login.gov
- FTC: Job scams
Try it now: Create (or sign in to) your USAJOBS profile. Run one search for a kind of job you could do in your area, add at least two filters, and save it. Write down how many jobs came up and the titles of three.
You can now set up a USAJOBS profile safely and save a search that sends you jobs that fit you.

check.q: A text says: "Apply for federal jobs here, $25 setup fee" with a link. What is true?
options: It is a scam: USAJOBS is free to use
It is fine if the link ends in .com
Federal jobs need a paid account
You should pay with a gift card to be safe
check.why: Searching and applying for federal jobs is always free, so anyone charging a fee is a scammer.

check.q: You want USAJOBS to tell you about new warehouse jobs near you. What do you do?
options: Search again every hour
Save the search and turn on email alerts
Ask a friend to watch the site
Create a new profile each week
check.why: A saved search with alerts emails you new jobs that match your filters.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading a federal job announcement
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the duties, qualifications, grade, closing date and required documents from an announcement.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real job announcement, you will list the duties, qualifications, grade, closing date and required documents, on a one-page summary sheet with none of the five missing.
Federal announcements are long, but they follow the same pattern. Near the top: the job title, agency, location, pay and grade, the open and closing dates, and who the job is open to. Then come sections such as Duties, Requirements (conditions of employment and qualifications), How you will be evaluated, Required documents and How to apply.
The most important part is Qualifications. Many jobs ask for specialized experience: experience doing the kind of work in the job, often described as one year at a level like the next lower grade. Some jobs let you qualify with education instead, or a mix of the two. Your resume must show this experience clearly, or you may be found not qualified.
Conditions of employment are rules you must meet to be hired, for example U.S. citizenship, passing a background check or a drug test, or holding a driver's license. Read them before you apply.
Watch the closing date. Some announcements also close early once they receive a set number of applications, so apply as soon as you are ready.
Step by step:
- Copy the job title, agency, announcement number, grade and pay.
- Copy the open and closing dates.
- Read "This job is open to".
- Copy the specialized experience or education you need.
- List the main duties.
- List every item in Required documents.
Words to know:
- Specialized experience: experience doing the kind of work the job needs, at the level the announcement asks for.
- Conditions of employment: rules you must meet to be hired, like citizenship or a background check.
- Closing date: the last day you can apply. Some jobs close early.
- Announcement number: the code that identifies one job posting; use it to track your application.
- Required documents: the papers the announcement says you must upload, such as a resume, transcripts or a DD-214.
Official sources:
- USAJOBS
- OPM: Federal hiring FAQ
Try it now: Pick one real announcement from your saved search that is open to you. On one sheet of paper make your announcement summary: title, agency, announcement number, grade and pay, closing date, who it is open to, the specialized experience in your own words, three main duties, and every required document.
You can now read a federal job announcement and pull out what you need on one page.

check.q: Which section tells you the experience your resume must show?
options: How to apply
Required documents
Next steps
Qualifications (specialized experience)
check.why: Qualifications describes the specialized experience or education you need to qualify.

check.q: An announcement closes on Friday but says it may close early. When should you apply?
options: As soon as your application is ready
On Friday at midnight
Next week
Only after the agency calls you
check.why: Jobs that may close early can stop taking applications before the closing date, so apply when you are ready.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a federal resume that matches the job
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write federal resume job entries that show the specialized experience the announcement asks for.
This lesson builds toward: Given the specialized experience an announcement asks for, you will write federal resume job entries with dates, hours per week, duties and results that match the announcement, using the announcement's key words and only true information.
A federal resume needs more detail than most private resumes. For each job, include the job title, the employer, the start and end dates (month and year) and the hours you worked per week. Agencies use dates and hours to count your experience, so a job without them may not count.
Under each job, write your duties and results in the announcement's own words. If the announcement asks for experience "maintaining inventory records", and you did that, write those words and add details: what you did, how much, how often and what got better. For example: "Kept inventory records for 1,200 items using a handheld scanner; cut count errors in half in six months."
Count all real experience: paid jobs, part-time work, military service, volunteer work and jobs held while incarcerated, such as kitchen, maintenance or clerk work. Be honest; never claim experience you do not have.
Read the announcement and the USAJOBS Help Center for any page limit or format rules, because they change. You can build a resume in USAJOBS or upload your own. If you use an AI tool to help with wording, leave out private numbers and check that every line is true.
Step by step:
- Copy the specialized experience sentence from your summary sheet.
- Pick the jobs where you did that kind of work.
- For each job, write the title, employer, start and end month and year, and hours per week.
- Write 3 to 5 lines of duties and results using the announcement's key words.
- Add a number to at least one line: how many, how much or how often.
- Check the announcement for page limits and read it all aloud for truth and spelling.
Words to know:
- Federal resume: a resume for a government job, with dates, hours per week and detailed duties for each job.
- Key words: the important words from the announcement that your resume should repeat where true.
- Result: what got better because of your work, best with a number.
- Hours per week: how many hours a week you worked in a job; agencies use it to count your experience.
Official sources:
- USAJOBS
- OPM FedsHireVets
Try it now: Using your announcement summary, write two federal resume job entries on paper or in a document. Each needs title, employer, month and year dates, hours per week, and 3 to 5 lines of duties and results that use the announcement's key words. Underline each key word you used.
You can now write federal resume entries with the dates, hours and matching experience an agency needs to count your work.

check.q: Which job entry is ready for a federal resume?
options: "Warehouse worker, did lots of stuff"
"Warehouse associate, ABC Supply, 03/2022 to 08/2024, 40 hours per week; kept inventory records for 1,200 items"
"Worked at a warehouse for a while"
"Hard worker, team player"
check.why: It has the title, employer, month and year dates, hours per week and a duty with a number.

check.q: The announcement asks for experience "operating a forklift". You drove a forklift while incarcerated. What do you do?
options: Leave it out because it does not count
Say you drove a forklift at a company you never worked for
Write only "general labor"
List it honestly with dates, hours and what you did
check.why: Real work experience counts, including work while incarcerated, when it is listed honestly with details.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The questionnaire and your documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Answer the questionnaire honestly and gather every document the announcement requires.
This lesson builds toward: Before you submit an application, you will answer the questionnaire honestly and collect every document the announcement requires, so each top-level answer is backed by your resume and no required document is missing.
Many announcements have an online questionnaire. You rate your own experience on tasks from the job, for example from "I have no experience" up to "I am an expert or have trained others". Your answers help decide whether you are qualified and how you rank.
Answer honestly, and make sure your resume backs up every high answer. If you say you are an expert at scheduling but your resume never mentions scheduling, a reviewer may lower your score or find you not qualified.
Then gather the documents in the Required documents section. Common ones: your resume; college transcripts if you qualify with education; for veterans a DD-214 that shows the character of service, plus an SF-15 or a VA letter if you claim 10-point preference; a Schedule A proof-of-disability letter if you apply under that path; and a recent personnel form (SF-50) for current or former federal employees. Upload clear, readable copies.
Some forms ask about criminal history. Federal law generally limits when agencies may ask before a conditional job offer, with exceptions for some jobs such as law enforcement. When you are asked, answer truthfully: false answers can cost you the job later. Check the announcement and OPM for the current rules, and ask a re-entry or legal aid program if you have questions.
Step by step:
- Read each questionnaire item slowly.
- Pick the answer that is true for you.
- For each high answer, find the resume line that backs it up; add one if the experience is real but missing.
- List every required document from your summary sheet.
- Write where you will get each one (for example: DD-214 from your records or the National Archives, transcripts from your school).
- Upload clear copies and check each one opens.
Words to know:
- Questionnaire: online questions where you rate your own experience on tasks from the job.
- DD-214: the paper that shows a veteran's dates and character of military service.
- SF-15: the form used to claim 10-point veterans' preference.
- Veterans' preference: extra consideration in federal hiring for eligible veterans.
- SF-50: a federal personnel form that shows a federal employee's job, grade and status.
- Conditional job offer: a job offer that depends on passing final checks, such as a background check.
Official sources:
- USAJOBS: Veterans hiring path (DD-214, SF-15, VA letter)
- OPM FedsHireVets: Veterans' preference
- USAJOBS: Explore hiring paths (Individuals with disabilities)
Try it now: Make a document checklist for your announcement with three columns: document, where I will get it, done. Then write three questionnaire-style tasks from the job's duties, rate yourself honestly on each, and next to each high rating write the resume line that proves it.
You can now answer a federal questionnaire honestly with your resume behind every answer, and gather all the documents the job asks for.

check.q: You rate yourself "expert" at scheduling, but your resume never mentions scheduling. What is likely?
options: The reviewer may lower your score or find you not qualified
Nothing; only the questionnaire counts
You will be hired faster
The agency will add it to your resume for you
check.why: Reviewers check that your resume supports your questionnaire answers.

check.q: A veteran is claiming 10-point preference. What should they upload, according to USAJOBS?
options: Only a resume
A letter from a friend
A DD-214 plus an SF-15 or an acceptable VA letter
A photo of their uniform
check.why: USAJOBS asks for a DD-214, and an SF-15 or other acceptable proof such as a VA letter for 10-point preference.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Submitting, tracking and staying safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track your application status in USAJOBS and spot fake government job offers.
This lesson builds toward: After you apply, you will track your application status and spot fake government job offers, keeping a dated log and never paying a fee or sharing private numbers outside USAJOBS. Given the specialized experience an announcement asks for, you will write federal resume job entries with dates, hours per week, duties and results that match the announcement, using the announcement's key words and only true information.
When you apply, USAJOBS sends you to the agency's application system to finish. Make sure you complete every step and get a confirmation; leaving after the questionnaire is a common reason an application never arrives.
Track every application in your USAJOBS profile. The status changes as the agency works: for example received, being reviewed, referred to the hiring manager or not referred, and later selected or not selected. Federal hiring can take weeks or months, so keep applying to other jobs while you wait. If you are not referred, read the notice and fix that part (often missing experience, dates or documents) for the next application.
Keep a simple log: job title, announcement number, agency, date applied, status and the next date you will check. Check about once a week.
Watch for scams. Applying for federal jobs is always free. Be careful with anyone who promises a government job for a fee, asks for payment or gift cards, asks for your Social Security or bank number by text or chat, or interviews you only by text. Real federal emails and websites end in .gov or .mil. If in doubt, type usajobs.gov yourself and check there.
Step by step:
- Finish every step in the agency system and save the confirmation.
- Start your application log.
- Check the status in USAJOBS about once a week.
- If not referred, read why and fix it next time.
- Never pay, and never send private numbers by text or chat.
Words to know:
- Referred: your application was sent to the hiring manager to consider.
- Not referred: your application was not sent on, often because the agency found you not qualified or other applicants ranked higher.
- Application log: your own list of jobs applied for, with dates and status.
- .gov: the web address ending used only by U.S. government agencies.
Official sources:
- FTC: Job scams (federal jobs are free to apply for)
- USAJOBS
Try it now: Final task: put your practice application packet together for your announcement: the one-page summary, at least two matching resume entries, the document checklist and an application log with the job number, the date you will apply and the next check date. Then read the packet against the rubric and fix one weak part.
You can now put together a complete federal application, track it, and keep yourself safe from fake job offers.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Job is open to you The chosen job is not open to any hiring path that fits the learner. The job is open to a hiring path that fits, and the summary names it. Also lists other paths the learner may use and one more open job. Announcement summary One or more of duties, qualifications, grade, closing date or required documents is missing. All five are on one page in the learner's own words. Also notes conditions of employment and whether the job may close early. Resume entries Entries lack month and year dates, hours per week or duties that match the job. Two or more entries with title, employer, dates, hours and duties using the announcement's key words. Every entry has at least one result with a number, and all lines are true and clear. Documents and questionnaire A required document is missing from the checklist, or a high self-rating has no resume line behind it. Every required document is listed with where to get it, and each high rating is backed by a resume line. Documents are already gathered and checked as readable. Tracking and safety No log, or the log or packet contains private numbers. A log with job number, dates, status and next check date; no private numbers. The learner can name three scam warning signs and how to check a job on usajobs.gov. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: Someone on social media offers you a guaranteed job at a federal agency for a $200 processing fee. What is this?
options: A normal federal hiring step
A way to skip the line legally
A scam: federal jobs are free to apply for
A fee USAJOBS charges veterans
check.why: The FTC says applying for federal jobs is always free and anyone charging for one is a scammer.

check.q: Your USAJOBS status says "Not referred". What is the best next step?
options: Stop applying for federal jobs
Read the notice and fix the weak part in your next application
Pay someone to change your status
Apply again to the same closed job
check.why: The notice often shows what was missing, so you can fix it next time.
